This group is not only a forum for coordination, rather it is the primary global, the primary forum of the developing world within the United Nations that is for negotiation. It is also a vital tool with which we can transform our political weight into the ability to influence and shape agendas. Against that backdrop, the ability to build agreements between countries with different points of view takes on particular significance. However, defending multilateralism does not mean championing the status quo. We need effective responses to the debt crisis, and we need to see ODA commitments upheld. South-South cooperation will continue to remain a tangible manifestation of solidarity and an expression of the fact that solutions must be built that are tailored to our realities. AI can expedite development, however, it can also widen divides. if we simply remain reduced to consumers. Since 1964, the G77 has spoken with a common voice. Together, you have championed development, driven South-South cooperation, strengthened multilateralism, including your support for the Pact for the Future, and provided vital leadership for key UN reforms. Excellencies, the G77 and China's quest for justice must continue. Conflicts are raging, ceasefires are broken, human rights and international law are flouted with impunity, climate chaos is worsening with another year of record-breaking heat, inequality is deepening, and progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals is lagging. Development is the ultimate driver of equality, human dignity, prosperity and peace. But declining official development assistance and falling trust and solidarity demand that we urgently find ways to protect the vision and goals of the 2030 Agenda. We must also recognize the clear need for peace. From the Middle East to Gaza, Sudan, Yemen and elsewhere, We need an end to the conflicts that are pushing development further out of reach. Excellencies, these converging challenges demand solutions grounded in justice. First, financial justice. Developing countries are drowning in debt. They need an additional $4 trillion per year to achieve the SDGs. Through the Seville Commitment, member states pledged to work to raise more domestic resources and to better channel them to areas of greatest need. But multilateral development banks must aggressively scale up investment. Bank shareholders must accelerate reforms, provide fresh capital, expand concessional finance, and unlock private investment. And we must increase the participation and weight of developing countries across the international financial architecture, bringing it in line with today's global economy and reforming adequately the international financial institutions. More than 100 G77 countries are supporting our spearheading initiatives under the Seville Platform for Action. And we need your leadership across our initiatives to make global economic governance more effective and inclusive, including the Borrower's Platform and the negotiations on the UN Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation. Second, climate justice. The climate crisis is hitting developing countries hardest. Extreme heat, floods, droughts, storms, and rising seas are destroying lives, livelihoods, and eroding hard-won development gains. Climate justice means protecting people before disasters strike, and standing with them as they recover and adapt. That requires a tripling of adaptation finance, far greater resources for loss and damage, accessible, predictable, and at the scale required. And every person on Earth being protected by an effective early warning system. Climate justice also means ensuring that developing countries benefit from the renewables revolution. Clean energy now attracts twice as much investment as fossil fuels, but the benefits are not being shared equally. The countries with some of the greatest renewable energy potential are receiving the least investment. Africa has 60% of the planet's best solar potential, but receives just 2% of global clean energy investments. Developing countries must be leaders and beneficiaries of the clean energy revolution not spectators. And that means affordable finance for renewables, grids, and storage. And it means justice in the responsible management of critical minerals, benefiting and adding value in producing countries first and foremost. As I usually say, no more plundering, no more exploitation. The clean energy transition must reduce global inequalities, not reproduce them. Third, technological justice. Artificial intelligence should benefit all countries, not just those that can afford it. We cannot let it perpetuate the inequalities and injustices that plague our world. I am grateful for the G77 support for the UN in establishing an independent international scientific panel and the Global Dialogue on AI Governance to give all countries an equal voice. And your support will be critical in establishing a Global Fund for AI Capacity Development. And fourth, justice through reform. From the start, the G77 and China have been strong and vocal supporters of our efforts to reform global institutions. For example, the United Nations Security Council and the Bretton Woods Institutions were created before many of your countries became independent. These systems do not reflect the voice, the influence, and the economic and political power that developing countries in particular now yield. They must be reformed. And you have been a wellspring of ideas and support as we move forward also with our UN80 initiative. This includes reforms to advance gender parity and to adjust this in geographic representation focus on country-level results and improves the effectiveness of our work. To expand countries' access to UN assets and knowledge across the system to deal with complex challenges and make progress on Agenda 2030. And to revitalize key UN bodies, including the committees of the General Assembly and ECOSOC. Every step of the way, we are working to respect the leadership of Member States and the principle of national ownership, all while maintaining a laser focus on the three core pillars of organization, peace and security, development, and human rights. I urge you to continue working with us as we finalize these reforms and ensure effective and impactful support of your priorities for decades to come. Excellencies, from the start, The G77 shown that narrow self-interest is no match for countries acting in solidarity. While this is my last meeting with your ministerial group as Secretary-General, I will always stand with you in your quest for justice, development, and peace. Thank you.

Laura Dubois, your Excellency, Laura Dubois, Permanent Representative of Uruguay to the United Nations and Chair of the Group of 77. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor to address this landmark 50th annual ministerial meeting of the Group of 77 in China. As someone from a G77 country, I know the group's enduring strength, its solidarity, its moral authority, and its capacity to give voice to the aspirations of the great majority of humanity. At a time of deepening mistrust, conflict, and inequality, the role of Global South is indispensable to sustaining the future of multilateralism. As President of the General Assembly, my overriding priority for this 81st session is to support the future of multilateralism by restoring trust, Trust among member states, and above all, trust in the United Nations as an institution capable of delivering for people. This requires renewed collective action. First, on peace and security, the United Nations must uphold the charter in its entirety in both letter and spirit. The Security Council bears primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. When it is able to discharge that responsibility effectively, impartially, and in accordance with the Charter, it bolsters public trust and confidence in our organization. Yet where the Council is unable to act, the Assembly must discharge its respective responsibility under the Charter and unfailingly adhere to the purposes and principles of the United Nations. The global south has also carried a large share of the burden of peacekeeping and peacebuilding. My country, Bangladesh, alone has contributed more than 200,000 peacekeepers over the years. This commitment must be matched by adequate mandates, predictable financing, political support, and a genuine focus on conflict prevention and sustainable peace. Second, on sustainable development, we have only four years left to deliver the 2030 agenda. Important progress notwithstanding, only 36% of SDG targets with available trend data are on track or making moderate progress. Nearly half, 49%, are moving too slowly, and 15% have slipped below their 2015 baselines. The financing environment has become even more difficult. Official development assistance fell by a record 23% in 2025. Global economic prospects offer little room for complacency. Persistent poverty and hunger, debt distress, climate shocks, and failing development assistance are putting hard-won progress at risk. We must close the financing gap. honor commitments, and accelerate implementation of the SDGs and Compromiso de Sevilla. The SDG Summit in 2027 will offer a crucial opportunity to assess implementation honestly, identify the barriers to delivery, and chart the steps needed beyond 2030. The climate outlook is equally stark. Under existing policies, we are on track for up to 2.8 degrees Celsius of warming this century, far beyond the 1.5 degree threshold we pledged to pursue. Climate change is already a daily reality for countries of the South. The recent catastrophic disaster in Nepal and China, triggered by a glacier-related collapse and devastating floods, is a stark warning of the cascading risks facing Himalayan communities and countries downstream. As warming destabilizes glaciers, permafrost, and mountain slopes, the threats of glacial lake outburst floods, landslides, water insecurity, and the destruction of critical infrastructure will grow. Adaptation, early warning systems, resilient infrastructure, disaster risk reduction, and adequately funded loss and damage arrangements must be central to our collective response. Third, We must also act with urgency on artificial intelligence. AI can help advance the sustainable development goals, but without effective norms and guardrails and independent oversight and human control, there is the danger that it may generate profound harm. AI governance must be inclusive, equitable, and development oriented, ensuring that AI narrows rather than widens the digital divide. Excellencies, on each of these issues, South-South cooperation is essential. Countries of the South are innovators, providers of practical technologies, and creators of solutions that can be adopted and scaled across regions. We must expand technology sharing, knowledge exchange, capacity building, and regional and interregional partnerships among countries of the South. Special and sustained support is essential for least developed countries, landlocked developing countries, small island developing states, and African countries. These countries face intersecting vulnerabilities, yet they also hold immense potential. Their priorities must be reflected in international financing, trade, technology, climate action, and global decision making. Excellencies, The future of multilateralism will be determined not by the number of declarations we adopt, but by whether we deliver meaningful results for the people we serve. The G77 and China has repeatedly demonstrated the power of collective action. I count on your leadership throughout this session to bridge divides, advance practical solutions, and ensure that the United Nations remains true to its charter and effectively deliver to all peoples, including peoples of the South. I thank you.

Mr. Chairman, Burkina Faso would like to express its gratitude to Uruguay for its commitment at the home of our group. The theme, the Global South and the future of multilateralism, resonates with the current challenges that our world faces. Today, the Global South represents the majority of the world's population and accounts for a growing share of global wealth. It also represents an immense reservoir of innovation and solutions, yet it still remains largely on the margins of development and global governance. The current multilateral architecture must therefore be readjusted so that the nations of the South can fully participate in shaping the rules that govern the international system. To this end, Burkina Faso would highlight four priorities. First, reform the international financial system to ensure more equitable access to development financing, and to provide sustainable solutions to debt-related challenges. Second, reform global governance so that international institutions better reflect the realities and the aspirations of the South. And third, move from a logic of aid to a logic of partnership based on co-creation, mutual respect, shared responsibility, and the end of dependency relationships. And 4th, preserve the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states. Terrorism, interference, and violations of sovereignty also constitute obstacles to development and to the aspirations of peoples. Under the leadership of the President of Burkina Faso, our country has chosen a development path based on a greater mobilization of its own domestic resources. The experience of the Confederation of Sahel States and its three member states demonstrates that unity and pooling capacities can strengthen our autonomy and our ability to act. We must therefore strengthen our solidarity and South-South cooperation in order to reduce dependencies and to better leverage our own potential. united within the group of 77 in China, we can contribute to building a more representative, more equitable and truly people-centered multilateralism, and I would like to conclude by addressing my heartfelt congratulations to Rwanda for its appointment as the chair of the G. 77, and assured of Burkina Faso's commitment, as well as that of the Confederation of Sahel States, to work towards consolidating the achievements made by our organization.
